title: COP31: Seas At Risk is calling for urgent action to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG)
summary: Seas At Risk's COP31 plea for "urgent action" against GHG and black carbon emissions starkly contrasts with shipping's slow transition from dirty fossil fuels. Scientific reports confirm a 1.5°C warming threshold is inevitable, yet the industry continues to offload its climate burden onto fragile marine ecosystems. Real emission reductions, not future carbon removal fantasies, are demanded from governments to hold the dirtiest ships accountable for their devastating environmental impact.
content:
As world leaders gather at COP31, Seas At Risk is calling for urgent action to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) and black carbon emissions to protect marine ecosystems and accelerate a fair transition away from fossil fuels in international shipping.

The latest scientific reports, such as the UNEP Emissions Gap Report, deliver a stark warning: exceeding the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C warming threshold is now inevitable. But how far that temperature rises, and for how long, depends upon governments making the right choices today.

The ocean is one of our biggest allies in the fight against climate change. It absorbs around 90% of the excess heat trapped by GHG, helping to regulate the earth’s climate. However, this comes at an enormous cost: rising ocean temperatures, marine heatwaves, acidification and mounting pressure on marine biodiversity.

Every fraction of a degree of warming increases these risks. Even if global temperatures return to 1.5 degrees after temporarily exceeding it, some damage to the marine environment could be irreversible.

COP31 must be about action, not just ambition. Governments must turn their commitments into real emission reductions, across all sectors, including shipping.

• Every fraction of a degree matters and the ocean cannot wait

Current climate policies are taking the world towards dangerous levels of warming. Even more ambitious pathways will temporarily exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius and depend upon intensified emission reductions and the uptake of clean fuels and technology.

For the ocean, any rise in warming spells danger. Marine ecosystems such as coral reefs, along with polar seas and coastal communities are on the forefront of escalating risks due to rising sea and atmosphere temperatures. Seas At Risk is calling for immediate intensification of efforts to reduce GHG emissions and deep cuts in emissions of methane and black carbon rather than relying on carbon removal which cannot be deployed at scale and must not replace efforts to decarbonise.

Seas At Risk is fighting for:

-A maritime sector that uptakes clean fuels and technologies such as wind propulsion,

-A rapid reduction in super pollutants like methane and black carbon, that is up to 1600 more warming and is destroying the Arctic,

-A healthy ocean that fights climate change. It naturally absorbs carbon, protects the coastline, feeds us and stabilises the weather,

-Funding, technology and international support for small islands, coastal communities, and low-income nations.

• The International Maritime Organization’s Net-Zero Framework: a critical opportunity for shipping climate action

International shipping cannot wait on the sidelines of global climate action.

As we get closer to critical discussions and decisions in December, the International Maritime Organization’s proposed Net-Zero Framework would establish global measures to reduce GHG emissions from ships, including a fuel GHG intensity standard and an economic mechanism.

Its implementation could help accelerate shipping’s transition towards cleaner energy, improve investment certainty and support international cooperation. Yet the framework, approved by IMO Member States in April 2025, is waiting to be adopted and remains politically contested. Any further delays, or weakening of the framework, beyond the next discussions at the IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee would postpone the introduction of global binding measures.

Seas At Risk is calling for an ambitious, effective and equitable IMO Net-Zero Framework, that deliver real emission reductions and includes a dedicated fund to support countries and communities facing disproportionate transition costs and the greatest climate impacts.
